AbstractText.Label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: We attempted to describe the opioid prescribing patterns for ambulatory pediatric surgery in the United States from 2007 to 2014.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Operating room ambulatory encounters as determined by the Truven Health Marketscan Commercial Claims and Encounters database.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 929,874 ambulatory surgical encounters were identified in patients <18years of age and, of these, 439,286 encounters generated an analgesic prescription.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTIONS
AbstractText.content: N/A MEASUREMENTS: The analgesic prescription was described in terms of the type of opioid along with the inclusion of acetaminophen and/or NSAIDs.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The probability of receiving a post-operative analgesic prescription increased with age, ranging from 18.2% of infants to 71.7% of teens. Acetaminophen with codeine (APAP/C) was the most common drug for infants (63.8%), while acetaminophen with hydrocodone (APAP/H) was the most common analgesic prescription for teens (53.6%). APAP/C and APAP/H were the predominant drugs used for all procedure types.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Substantial variability in analgesic prescribing at the level of the procedure performed, both in terms of the probability of receiving a prescription and in which drugs were prescribed. We observed significant age and procedure-based variability in opioid prescribing following pediatric ambulatory surgery.
